AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework for incorporating knowledge into multimodal generative models by identifying four intervention layers: surface, trajectory, latent, and parametric infusion.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for incorporating knowledge into generative models are typically categorized by technique rather than by the component of the generative process they modify, and the authors argue that knowledge infusion in iterative generative models is fundamentally an intervention-layer problem.
AI.method: The authors instantiate their framework in diffusion models, map representative methods to all four layers, and derive design principles for multi-layer composition.
AI.result: The authors show empirically that each additional layer addresses failure classes that prior layers cannot reach, reducing knowledge-violating outputs by 70.97% compared to vanilla generation.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the proposed framework provides a comprehensive approach to incorporating knowledge into multimodal generative models, and that the four intervention layers can be composed to improve the reliability of generated outputs.

title: Visual Commonsense Driven Knowledge Refinements for Scene Graph Generation
summary: Learning-driven Scene Graph Generation (SGG) models excel on frequent relation types but degrade sharply under annotation sparsity, failing to capture reliable visual commonsense knowledge. We propose a model-agnostic, semantically-guided knowledge refinement framework that systematically mines commonsense-grounded constraints from training data - capturing spatial, functional, and qualitative relational regularities - and uses general declarative commonsense reasoning to correct and refine ranked SGG predictions at inference time. The framework requires no manual rule authoring, no model retraining, and transfers across datasets and architectures. On three standard benchmarks, we obtain consistent improvements over strong baselines, demonstrating that structured visual commonsense reasoning over deep scene semantics is a practical and effective complement to purely learning-based scene graph generation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a model-agnostic framework that uses commonsense knowledge to improve scene graph generation, particularly under sparse annotations.
AI.motivation: Existing scene graph generation models perform well on frequent relation types but degrade under annotation sparsity, lacking reliable visual commonsense knowledge.
AI.method: A semantically-guided knowledge refinement framework that mines commonsense-grounded constraints and uses declarative commonsense reasoning to refine SGG predictions.
AI.result: The framework achieves consistent improvements over strong baselines on three standard benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a practical and effective complement to purely learning-based scene graph generation by incorporating structured visual commonsense reasoning.

title: CollabSim: A CSCW-Grounded Methodology for Investigating Collaborative Competence of LLM Agents through Controlled Multi-Agent Experiments
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models have shown growing promise, with their effectiveness resting on agents' ability to coordinate through text-based channels much as human teams do. Yet recent study suggests that MAS often falter not because agents lack individual task-solving ability, but because they lack collaborative competence: the capacity to establish common ground, maintain shared task understanding, balance individual and collective incentives, and repair misalignment as interaction unfolds. Decades of research in Computer-Supported Cooperative Work have characterized these requirements for human teams coordinating under constrained communication, yet existing MAS evaluations focus mainly on task outcomes or single-agent proficiency in reasoning, planning, and tool use. To enable a systematic analysis of agents' collaborative competence in MAS, we introduce CollabSim, a configurable simulation framework that combines a theory-grounded definition of collaborative capabilities, controlled manipulation of interaction conditions, and action-level probing of agents' internal states. Experiments across four LLMs show that CollabSim can capture condition effects, separate model performance patterns, and reveal task-dependent effects of agent design.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CollabSim, a simulation framework to analyze the collaborative competence of multi-agent systems built on large language models, which is crucial for their effectiveness.
AI.motivation: The effectiveness of multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models rests on agents' ability to coordinate through text-based channels, but they often falter due to lack of collaborative competence.
AI.method: The authors introduce CollabSim, a configurable simulation framework that combines a theory-grounded definition of collaborative capabilities, controlled manipulation of interaction conditions, and action-level probing of agents' internal states.
AI.result: Experiments across four LLMs show that CollabSim can capture condition effects, separate model performance patterns, and reveal task-dependent effects of agent design.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that CollabSim enables a systematic analysis of agents' collaborative competence in MAS, which is essential for improving their effectiveness.

title: An Infectious Disease Spread Simulation Based on Large Language Model Decision Making
summary: Modelling individual decision-making during infectious disease outbreaks is crucial for understanding behavioural dynamics and informing effective public health interventions. Prior work has shown that large language models can simulate realistic human behaviour by generating agent decisions based on demographic prompts and situational context. We build on this foundation with a spatially grounded, agent-based simulation framework that integrates LLM-generated decisions about self-reported influenza-like illness into a census-based synthetic population of agents. Location is treated as a central feature: agents are assigned to spatial units within cities, capturing the spatial distributions of different demographic groups using real-world census data and enabling geographically diverse behavioural modelling. We implement and compare three decision scenarios, independent reasoning, household influence, and message framing, and simulate self-reporting outcomes in San Francisco and Atlanta. Results reveal that income and education are the dominant drivers of reporting rate variation, with smaller but consistent effects from geography, LLM model choice, and message framing. Our framework generates synthetic data that captures both social and geographic heterogeneity, supporting spatial epidemiological modelling and bias-aware behavioural analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a spatially grounded agent-based simulation framework that uses large language models to simulate human behavior during infectious disease outbreaks, focusing on self-reported influenza-like illness in San Francisco and Atlanta.
AI.motivation: To understand behavioral dynamics during infectious disease outbreaks and inform effective public health interventions by simulating realistic human behavior.
AI.method: A spatially grounded, agent-based simulation framework integrating LLM-generated decisions into a census-based synthetic population, capturing spatial distributions of demographic groups and geographically diverse behavioral modeling.
AI.result: Income and education are the dominant drivers of reporting rate variation, with smaller but consistent effects from geography, LLM model choice, and message framing.
AI.conclusion: The framework generates synthetic data capturing social and geographic heterogeneity, supporting spatial epidemiological modeling and bias-aware behavioral analysis.

title: EasyLens: A Training-Free Plug-and-Play Subtle-Lesion Representation Amplifier for Medical Vision-Language Models
summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) have shown increasing potential for clinical image interpretation, including lesion detection and report generation. However, their practical utility remains limited by insufficient sensitivity to subtle lesions, whose visual evidence is often sparse, low-contrast, and embedded within complex anatomical context. As local visual tokens are aggregated, these weak lesion cues can become underrepresented in global image representations, making them difficult for medical VLMs to recognize. Existing efforts to improve lesion sensitivity mainly rely on medical-domain vision-encoder pre-training, clinical-term-guided alignment, or trainable pathological representation enhancement. Although effective, these approaches usually require additional training or model-specific adaptation and may overfit to particular disease morphologies, limiting their applicability to frozen medical VLMs. To address these limitations, we propose EasyLens, a training-free plug-and-play subtle-lesion representation amplifier for medical VLMs. EasyLens first constructs EasyBank, a pathology-anatomy prototype space that provides lesion-related prototypes and anatomy-aware normal references for comparing suspicious patches against both pathological and normal anatomical patterns. To avoid blindly amplifying normal tissues, EasyTag selects lesion-relevant patches through counterfactual prototype reasoning. To counteract the dilution of subtle lesion cues in global image representations, EasyAmplifier strengthens the selected lesion-relevant patch representations through morphology-guided residual enhancement, thereby increasing their contribution to the global image embedding. Experiments on multiple medical image datasets and frozen medical VLM backbones show that EasyLens improves subtle-lesion detection and outperforms existing encoder-enhancement baselines.

AI.tldr: A new method called EasyLens is proposed to improve the sensitivity of medical vision-language models to subtle lesions in images without requiring additional training.
AI.motivation: Current medical vision-language models have limited practical utility due to insufficient sensitivity to subtle lesions, which can be sparse, low-contrast, and embedded in complex anatomical contexts.
AI.method: EasyLens is a training-free plug-and-play approach that constructs a pathology-anatomy prototype space (EasyBank) and uses counterfactual prototype reasoning (EasyTag) to select lesion-relevant patches, then strengthens these patch representations through morphology-guided residual enhancement (EasyAmplifier).
AI.result: Experiments on multiple medical image datasets and frozen medical VLM backbones show that EasyLens improves subtle-lesion detection and outperforms existing encoder-enhancement baselines.
AI.conclusion: EasyLens offers a promising solution to enhance the sensitivity of medical vision-language models to subtle lesions without requiring additional training or model-specific adaptation.

title: A Komi-Yazva--Russian Parallel Corpus and Evaluation Protocol for Zero- and Few-Shot LLM Translation
summary: We present the first Komi-Yazva--Russian parallel corpus together with an explicit evaluation protocol for studying LLM translation in an endangered, extremely low-resource setting. The dataset contains 457 aligned sentence pairs from 74 narrative texts and is accompanied by documented provenance, sentence-level alignment, and story identifiers that enable leakage-aware evaluation. We use this setup to compare modern large language models on Komi-Yazva-to-Russian translation under severe parallel-data scarcity in zero-shot and retrieval-based few-shot regimes. The protocol includes story-level cross-validation, deterministic retrieval for few-shot prompting, strict validation of generated outputs, complementary reference-based and judge-based metrics, and story-level uncertainty estimates. Across models, LLMs produce non-trivial translations, but performance varies strongly by model family and prompting regime. Retrieval-based few-shot prompting consistently improves over zero-shot prompting, while gains beyond a small retrieved context remain limited. The results show that evaluative conclusions in this setting depend materially on metric choice and failure handling, so the paper frames the corpus as both a dataset contribution and a reproducible evaluation testbed for endangered-language machine translation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a parallel corpus for Komi-Yazva-Russian translation and evaluates large language models in a low-resource setting.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of machine translation for endangered languages with extremely limited parallel data.
AI.method: The authors create a parallel corpus with 457 aligned sentence pairs and develop an evaluation protocol including story-level cross-validation and retrieval-based few-shot prompting.
AI.result: Large language models produce non-trivial translations, with performance varying by model family and prompting regime; retrieval-based few-shot prompting improves over zero-shot prompting.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a dataset and evaluation testbed for endangered-language machine translation, highlighting the importance of metric choice and failure handling.

title: Rethinking Infrastructure Inspection as Image Difference Classification: A Traffic Sign Case Study
comment: CVPR 2026 Computer Vision for the Built World Workshop (CV4AEC @ CVPR)
summary: Digital twins (DTs) allow the digitalization of road infrastructure inspection, though this is hindered by limited annotated data. This work exploits the relational nature of continuous asset condition monitoring to reformulate image-based defect detection as image difference classification (IDC) to reduce data reliance. This was evaluated in a case study on low-resource traffic sign inspection with different IDC classifiers using a newly-curated, high quality dataset. Results indicate that the instruction-based classifier outperforms encoder-based ones and gains from comparison with reference images. This shows that IDC can be an effective task modeling for tackling data constraints in infrastructure inspection and DT asset condition updating.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using image difference classification to improve data efficiency in digital twin-based road infrastructure inspection.
AI.motivation: The limited availability of annotated data hinders the digitalization of road infrastructure inspection using digital twins.
AI.method: The authors reformulate image-based defect detection as image difference classification (IDC) and evaluate it using a newly curated dataset for traffic sign inspection.
AI.result: The instruction-based classifier outperforms encoder-based ones, and using reference images improves results, showing IDC's effectiveness in tackling data constraints.
AI.conclusion: IDC can be an effective approach for modeling tasks in infrastructure inspection and updating digital twin asset conditions with limited data.

title: HomeWorld: A Unified Floorplan-to-Furnished Framework for Generating Controllable, Densely Interactive Whole-Home Scenes
summary: Indoor scene generation is crucial for robot simulation and modern interior design. However, complex layouts together with scarce 3D scene data make learning-based generation challenging. Existing methods often rely on hand-crafted rules or focus on isolated sub-tasks (e.g., floorplan synthesis or single-room furnishing), producing whole-home scenes that lack global coherence, realism, and simulation readiness. To mitigate these limitations, we propose a unified hierarchical framework that decomposes indoor scene synthesis into controllable stages. First, we curate a large-scale dataset of 300K real residential floorplans to train a large language model for whole-home floorplan generation. With detailed descriptions and a K-D tree-based representation, our method enables fine-grained, controllable whole-home floorplan generation. Building upon the generated whole-home floorplan, we leverage image generation models to draft furniture layouts from multi-level roaming viewpoints, and then generate the layouts of small manipulable objects on different supporting surfaces (e.g., cabinets, desks, and dining tables) for embodied AI simulation. During furniture and object layout generation, a VLM-based refiner iteratively corrects furniture and object placement, and a 3D generative model enables flexible replacement of individual assets. We further attach basic physical attributes and simple surface texture and lighting setups to complete the pipeline for embodied AI use. Experiments and user studies demonstrate that our pipeline produces indoor spaces with greater layout diversity and stronger 3D design appeal, outperforming prior methods on both quantitative and qualitative metrics. Finally, alongside our generation pipeline, we will release the floorplan dataset and 5K fully furnished scenes to the community. Project Page: https://kairos-homeworld.github.io/

AI.tldr: A unified hierarchical framework for generating indoor scenes with controllable stages, producing diverse and realistic whole-home scenes for robot simulation and interior design.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for indoor scene generation rely on hand-crafted rules or focus on isolated sub-tasks, producing scenes that lack global coherence, realism, and simulation readiness.
AI.method: A multi-stage framework: (1) training a large language model for whole-home floorplan generation using a large-scale dataset, (2) generating furniture layouts from multi-level roaming viewpoints, and (3) generating small object layouts with a VLM-based refiner and 3D generative model.
AI.result: The proposed pipeline produces indoor spaces with greater layout diversity and stronger 3D design appeal, outperforming prior methods on both quantitative and qualitative metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified hierarchical framework enables the generation of realistic and diverse whole-home scenes, and the released dataset and furnished scenes can benefit the community.

title: Reinforcement Learning Elicits Contextual Learning of Unseen Language Translation
summary: Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) can translate unseen or low-resource languages by undergoing continued training or even by encoding a grammar book in their context. However, both methods typically overfit specific languages, with limited zero-shot transfer at test time. To translate extremely low-resource languages at scale, we argue that LLMs must acquire the meta-skill of utilizing in-context linguistic knowledge rather than memorizing specific languages. In this paper, we propose a reinforcement learning (RL) approach to unseen language translation given rich linguistic context, using a surface-level translation metric (chrF) as the reward. Empirically, despite the lightweight reward, our RL-trained models effectively extract and apply relevant linguistic information from the provided context, leading to better translations on completely unseen languages than in-context learning or supervised fine-tuning. Our analyses suggest that outcome-based RL can extend beyond conventional reasoning tasks like math and coding to serve as a recipe for language learning from context.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a reinforcement learning approach to translate low-resource languages using large language models and linguistic context.
AI.motivation: Current methods for translating low-resource languages using large language models often overfit to specific languages and have limited zero-shot transfer capabilities.
AI.method: A reinforcement learning approach using a surface-level translation metric (chrF) as the reward to train models for unseen language translation.
AI.result: The RL-trained models effectively extract and apply relevant linguistic information from context, leading to better translations on unseen languages.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach enables large language models to acquire the meta-skill of utilizing in-context linguistic knowledge for translation.

title: Humans' ALMANAC: A Human Collaboration Dataset of Action-Level Mental Model Annotations for Agent Collaboration
summary: Recent advances in LLM agents have enabled complex cognitive capabilities, such as multi-step reasoning, planning, and tool use, that increasingly position these agents as human collaborators. Effective collaboration, however, requires collaborators to continuously maintain and align mental models of their own reasoning,partners' intentions, and shared goals during the collaborative process. Today's agents rarely develop such capabilities since they are primarily optimized for task completion, and the community lacks authentic human collaboration data with action-level mental model annotations that could guide agents toward process-level collaborative competence. To bridge this gap, we present ALMANAC, a dataset of Action-Level Mental model ANnotations for Agent Collaboration built from the Map Task, a classic dyadic routing task from social science. ALMANAC contains 2,987 collaboration actions, each paired with theory-informed mental model annotations that record the participants' self-reasoning, perceived partner intent, and perceived team goal. We benchmark six LLMs on predicting humans' next-turn behavior and mental models. Our results demonstrate ALMANAC's utility in evaluating models' ability to simulate human collaborative behaviors and infer their underlying mental models.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ALMANAC, a dataset for training LLM agents to collaborate with humans by predicting their mental models and behavior.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to enable LLM agents to effectively collaborate with humans by developing capabilities to maintain and align mental models of their own reasoning, partners' intentions, and shared goals.
AI.method: The authors create a dataset called ALMANAC, which contains 2,987 collaboration actions with mental model annotations, and benchmark six LLMs on predicting humans' next-turn behavior and mental models.
AI.result: The results demonstrate ALMANAC's utility in evaluating models' ability to simulate human collaborative behaviors and infer their underlying mental models.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that ALMANAC can be used to improve LLM agents' ability to collaborate with humans by developing more sophisticated mental models and behaviors.

title: A Vision-language Framework for Comparative Reasoning in Radiology
summary: Medical imaging artificial intelligence has achieved strong performance in isolated image interpretation, but remains poorly aligned with radiological practice, where diagnosis and follow-up rely on comparison across prior studies and analogous reference cases. Here we formulate radiological comparison as an entity-aware cross-image reasoning problem and introduce a framework that supports both reference-case retrieval and temporal comparative interpretation. We construct MedReCo-DB, a large-scale comparative imaging resource derived from routine image-report pairs, comprising more than 690,000 images from over 160,000 patients across eight institutions, four countries and seven imaging modalities. Reports are decomposed into anatomical structures, abnormal findings and pathological conditions to provide supervision for entity-conditioned retrieval and comparative visual question answering. Using this resource, we develop MedReCo, an entity-aware visual encoder for controllable retrieval of clinically analogous cases, and MedReCo-VLM, a vision--language extension for generative interpretation of interval change. Across internal, external and cross-center evaluations, MedReCo achieved the highest Recall@1 in all 12 internal retrieval settings and improved external retrieval by a mean of 6.0 percentage points. In clinically confusable differential groups, it consistently outperformed the strongest baselines. MedReCo-VLM achieved the best performance across all comparative generation evaluations and improved longitudinal follow-up accuracy by 14.5-46.5 percentage points on chest radiographs and 13.0-27.9 percentage points on CT. These findings suggest that entity-aware comparative reasoning can be learned from routine clinical data at scale and may provide a more clinically aligned foundation for medical imaging AI.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a framework for radiological comparison in medical imaging AI, introducing entity-aware cross-image reasoning for reference-case retrieval and temporal comparative interpretation.
AI.motivation: Current medical imaging AI struggles to align with radiological practice, which relies on comparison across prior studies and reference cases.
AI.method: The authors construct a large-scale comparative imaging resource (MedReCo-DB) and develop two models: MedReCo for entity-aware visual encoding and MedReCo-VLM for generative interpretation of interval change.
AI.result: MedReCo and MedReCo-VLM outperform baselines in retrieval and comparative generation evaluations, with improvements in recall and longitudinal follow-up accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Entity-aware comparative reasoning can be learned from routine clinical data at scale, providing a more clinically aligned foundation for medical imaging AI.

title: Revising Context, Shifting Simulated Stance: Auditing LLM-Based Stance Simulation in Online Discussions
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate social media users and infer how individuals may respond to online discussions. However, it remains unclear whether these simulations reflect precise user-specific beliefs or whether they are highly sensitive to semantically independent changes in conversational contexts. In this work, we study counterfactual context revision as a framework for auditing LLM-based stance simulation. Given an original online conversation, we first infer a target user's stance toward a specific topic. We then apply controlled revision strategies to the conversational context and simulate the user's stance again under the revised context. We compare text-only revision strategies with a multimodal one that incorporates meme-based context and evaluate two main effectiveness metrics, i.e., average directional stance shift and stance transition rate. The results reveal effective and robust stance transitions in both text-only and multimodal strategies across different polarization-preference mechanisms. Our study contributes an evaluation framework for understanding the context sensitivity of LLM-based stance simulation. More broadly, it highlights both the promise and risk of using LLMs to simulate online opinion dynamics.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates the context sensitivity of large language models (LLMs) in simulating user stances in online discussions by applying counterfactual context revisions.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLM-based simulations of user stances are sensitive to changes in conversational contexts and to evaluate the effectiveness of different revision strategies.
AI.method: The study uses a framework of counterfactual context revision, applying text-only and multimodal revision strategies to simulate user stances in online conversations.
AI.result: The results show effective and robust stance transitions in both text-only and multimodal strategies, highlighting the context sensitivity of LLM-based stance simulation.
AI.conclusion: The study contributes an evaluation framework for understanding the context sensitivity of LLM-based stance simulation and highlights both the promise and risk of using LLMs to simulate online opinion dynamics.

title: Risk Assessment of Autonomous Driving: Integrating Technical Failures, Ethical Dilemmas, and Policy Frameworks
summary: Autonomous driving technology has the potential to reduce the large number of road traffic accidents caused by human error each year, but it also brings new types of risks that need to be evaluated from the aspects of technology, ethics and regulations. Based on public crash data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), disengagement reports from the California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV), the MIT Moral Machines dataset, and a comparative regulatory analysis of five jurisdictions, we have found that the main types of technical failure modes are perception and classification errors. These account for a relatively large proportion of the reported accidents, and it can be concluded that there are different ethical frameworks for autonomous vehicle decision-making, and inconsistent regulations in different areas increase the uncertainty of widespread application. Generally speaking, the problems of technology, ethics and regulation are closely related and need to be solved together. Therefore, this paper recommends a more adaptive and cooperative governance approach that combines engineering standards, ethical discussion, and institutional supervision.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes risks associated with autonomous driving, identifying technical failure modes and ethical frameworks, and recommends a cooperative governance approach.
AI.motivation: Autonomous driving technology has the potential to reduce road traffic accidents caused by human error, but it also brings new types of risks that need to be evaluated.
AI.method: The study uses public crash data from NHTSA, disengagement reports from DMV, the MIT Moral Machines dataset, and a comparative regulatory analysis of five jurisdictions.
AI.result: The main types of technical failure modes are perception and classification errors, and there are different ethical frameworks for autonomous vehicle decision-making and inconsistent regulations.
AI.conclusion: The problems of technology, ethics, and regulation are closely related and need to be solved together, and a more adaptive and cooperative governance approach is recommended.

title: Thinking with Imagination: Agentic Visual Spatial Reasoning with World Simulators
summary: While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have shown strong visual reasoning capabilities, their spatial reasoning abilities remain largely constrained to the observed images and text-oriented chain-of-thought. They often struggle to infer unobserved layouts, maintain cross-view consistency, and reason from alternative viewpoints when only limited egocentric observations are available. In this work, we study this problem as thinking with imagination, where a VLM actively acquires imagined visual evidence by interacting with a world simulator during reasoning. We propose Astra, an agentic spatial reasoning framework that empowers VLMs with action-conditioned visual imagination. Specifically, Astra couples Astra-VL, an RL-trained VLM policy, with Astra-WM, a Bagel-based world simulator that generates novel-view observations from context images and natural-language camera motions. To provide reliable imagined evidence, Astra-WM is trained with view consistency tuning to improve pose and content consistency across views. In the RL stage, we propose a world-simulator-in-the-loop two-phase RL curriculum to stabilize tool-use exploration and advance the model's ability to invoke the simulator only when imagined observations improve over direct answering. Experiments demonstrate that both the world simulator and the agentic policy are necessary: Astra-WM improves simulator-augmented Gemini-3-Flash on MMSI-Bench from 45.1 to 49.5, while Astra-VL improves the Qwen3-VL backbone from 29.8 to 38.8 on MMSI-Bench and from 36.8 to 42.7 on MindCube. These results show that imagined observations can provide useful spatial evidence, but effective world-model-augmented reasoning requires learning when, where, and how to imagine.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Astra, a framework that enhances Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with spatial reasoning capabilities by incorporating imagined visual evidence through interaction with a world simulator.
AI.motivation: Current VLMs are limited in their spatial reasoning abilities, particularly in inferring unobserved layouts, maintaining cross-view consistency, and reasoning from alternative viewpoints with limited observations.
AI.method: The Astra framework consists of Astra-VL, an RL-trained VLM policy, and Astra-WM, a world simulator that generates novel-view observations. Astra-WM is trained with view consistency tuning, and Astra-VL is trained with a two-phase RL curriculum that stabilizes tool-use exploration.
AI.result: Experiments show that Astra improves the performance of VLMs on MMSI-Bench and MindCube benchmarks, with Astra-WM improving Gemini-3-Flash from 45.1 to 49.5 and Astra-VL improving Qwen3-VL backbone from 29.8 to 38.8 and 36.8 to 42.7 respectively.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that imagined observations can provide useful spatial evidence, but effective world-model-augmented reasoning requires learning when, where, and how to imagine.

title: Latent Reasoning with Normalizing Flows
summary: Large language models often improve reasoning by generating explicit chain-of-thought (CoT), demonstrating the importance of intermediate computation. However, textual CoT forces this computation through a discrete, serial, and communication-oriented token stream: each reasoning step must be verbalized before the model can proceed, even when the underlying update is semantic, uncertain, or only partially formed. Latent reasoning offers a higher-bandwidth alternative by performing intermediate computation in compact continuous states before committing to text. Yet existing latent-reasoning methods often sacrifice key advantages that make CoT effective in autoregressive language models, including native left-to-right generation, probabilistic sampling, compatibility with KV-cache decoding, and tractable likelihood estimation. We propose NF-CoT, a latent reasoning framework that preserves these advantages by modeling continuous thoughts with normalizing flows. NF-CoT instantiates a TARFlow-style normalizing flow inside the LLM backbone, defining a tractable probability model over compact continuous thoughts distilled from explicit CoT. Continuous-thought positions are generated by an NF head, while text positions are generated by the standard LM head within the same causal stream. This design provides exact likelihoods for latent thoughts, enables probabilistic left-to-right decoding with the original KV cache, and supports direct policy-gradient optimization in the latent reasoning space. On code-generation benchmarks, NF-CoT improves pass rates over explicit-CoT and prior latent-reasoning baselines while substantially reducing intermediate-reasoning cost.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes NF-CoT, a latent reasoning framework that enables large language models to perform intermediate computation in compact continuous states, improving reasoning efficiency while preserving key advantages of chain-of-thought (CoT) methods.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to address the limitations of textual chain-of-thought (CoT) methods, which force computation through a discrete, serial, and communication-oriented token stream, and existing latent-reasoning methods that sacrifice key advantages of CoT.
AI.method: The authors propose NF-CoT, a latent reasoning framework that models continuous thoughts with normalizing flows, instantiating a TARFlow-style normalizing flow inside the LLM backbone, and defining a tractable probability model over compact continuous thoughts distilled from explicit CoT.
AI.result: NF-CoT improves pass rates over explicit-CoT and prior latent-reasoning baselines on code-generation benchmarks while substantially reducing intermediate-reasoning cost.
AI.conclusion: The proposed NF-CoT framework offers a higher-bandwidth alternative to textual CoT methods, enabling more efficient and effective reasoning in large language models.

title: Unsupervised Skill Discovery for Agentic Data Analysis
summary: Inference-time skill augmentation provides a lightweight way to improve data-analytic agents by injecting reusable procedural knowledge without updating model parameters. However, discovering effective skills for data analysis remains challenging, as reliable supervision is expensive and success criteria vary across analytical formats. This raises the key question of how to discover reusable data-analysis skills from unlabeled exploration alone. We propose DataCOPE, an unsupervised verifier-guided skill discovery framework for data-analytic agents. DataCOPE derives verifier signals from the exploration trajectories and uses them to characterize relative quality or aggreement among trajectories. It iteratively coordinates a Data-Analytic Agent for trajectory generation, an Unsupervised Verifier for signal extraction, and a Skill Manager for contrastive skill distillation. For report-style analysis, we instantiate the verifier as an Adaptive Checklist Verifier that derives task-specific criteria, scores reports by verifiable coverage, and iteratively refines the checklist. For reasoning-style analysis, we instantiate it as an Answer Agreement Verifier that groups trajectories by answer agreement and uses self-consistency as an auxiliary signal. We evaluate DataCOPE on report-style analysis from Deep Data Research and reasoning-style analysis from DABStep. Across both settings, DataCOPE consistently improves held-out performance over baselines. Averaged across four model settings, DataCOPE improves the mean score by 9.71% and 32.30% on report-style and reasoning-style tasks respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DataCOPE, a framework for discovering reusable data-analysis skills from unlabeled exploration, improving data-analytic agents without updating model parameters.
AI.motivation: The challenge of discovering effective skills for data analysis due to the lack of reliable supervision and varying success criteria across analytical formats.
AI.method: DataCOPE, an unsupervised verifier-guided skill discovery framework, which uses verifier signals to characterize trajectory quality and iteratively coordinates a Data-Analytic Agent, Unsupervised Verifier, and Skill Manager.
AI.result: DataCOPE consistently improves held-out performance over baselines, with an average improvement of 9.71% on report-style tasks and 32.30% on reasoning-style tasks.
AI.conclusion: DataCOPE provides a effective way to discover reusable data-analysis skills from unlabeled exploration, improving data-analytic agents without updating model parameters.

title: Complexity-Balanced Diffusion Splitting
summary: Standard continuous-time generative models rely on monolithic architectures that must navigate vastly different signal regimes, from isotropic noise to intricate data distributions. While scaling model capacity improves performance, deploying a massive network uniformly across the entire generative timeline is inherently inefficient. In this work, we propose Complexity-Balanced Splitting (CBS), a principled framework for temporal capacity allocation that distributes the generative workload across multiple specialized sub-networks. Grounded in function approximation theory and de Boor's equidistribution principle, CBS partitions the diffusion timeline into segments of equal approximation burden, allocating more representational capacity to regions where the generative dynamics are more difficult to model. To estimate this local complexity, we introduce two complementary and tractable monitor functions: a spatial measure based on the flow's Dirichlet energy, and a geometric measure based on the acceleration of the sampling trajectories. Using a lightweight auxiliary model to estimate these complexity profiles, our approach eliminates the need for heuristic temporal splits or computationally expensive search procedures. Extensive evaluation across multiple architectures (SiT, JiT, and UNet) and datasets demonstrates that CBS consistently improves synthesis quality without increasing per-step inference cost. In particular, CBS improves FID by ~35% on SiT-XL with CFG relative to naive temporal partitioning. Project page is available at https://noamissachar.github.io/CBS/.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Complexity-Balanced Splitting (CBS), a framework for temporal capacity allocation in generative models, which distributes workload across specialized sub-networks.
AI.motivation: Current generative models use monolithic architectures that are inefficient when dealing with different signal regimes, and scaling model capacity uniformly is not optimal.
AI.method: CBS uses function approximation theory and de Boor's equidistribution principle to partition the diffusion timeline into segments of equal approximation burden, allocating more capacity to complex regions.
AI.result: CBS consistently improves synthesis quality without increasing per-step inference cost, with a ~35% improvement in FID on SiT-XL with CFG.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework, CBS, offers a principled approach to temporal capacity allocation, leading to improved performance in generative models.

title: Human Adults and LLMs as Scientists: Who Benefits from Active Exploration?
comment: Accepted at the 48th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society (CogSci 2026)
summary: A long-standing finding in the causal learning literature is that adults struggle to identify conjunctive causal rules, where an effect requires the simultaneous presence of multiple causes, while performing better in disjunctive settings. However, most demonstrations of this ``conjunctive handicap'' rely on passive observation paradigms with limited evidence, where learners have no control over evidence generation. This paper asks whether this bias persists when adults are granted agency through active exploration. Using a modified ``blicket detector'' task, adult participants freely intervened to identify causal objects under conjunctive or disjunctive rule structures. We show that active exploration substantially improves adults' conjunctive causal reasoning, although conjunctive rules still require more tests to infer than disjunctive rules. We further compare human performance to a range of large language models in the same setting. While some state-of-the-art models approach human-level performance on hypothesis inference accuracy, they often exhibit less efficient exploration strategies and similar conjunctive-disjunctive performance gaps.

AI.tldr: Adults' ability to identify conjunctive causal rules improves with active exploration, but still lags behind disjunctive settings; large language models approach human-level accuracy but have less efficient exploration strategies.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether adults' difficulty in identifying conjunctive causal rules persists when they are granted agency through active exploration, and to compare human performance with large language models.
AI.method: A modified 'blicket detector' task was used, where adult participants freely intervened to identify causal objects under conjunctive or disjunctive rule structures.
AI.result: Active exploration substantially improves adults' conjunctive causal reasoning, but conjunctive rules still require more tests to infer than disjunctive rules; large language models approach human-level performance on hypothesis inference accuracy but exhibit less efficient exploration strategies.
AI.conclusion: The study suggests that granting adults agency through active exploration can improve their conjunctive causal reasoning, but does not eliminate the conjunctive-disjunctive performance gap; large language models can match human accuracy but have room for improvement in exploration efficiency.

title: Agent Memory: Characterization and System Implications of Stateful Long-Horizon Workloads
summary: LLM agents are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks requiring sustained reasoning over extended interaction histories. Realizing this at scale requires agents to persistently store, retrieve, and update their own memory across sessions. A rich ecosystem of agent memory systems has emerged spanning flat retrieval, LLM-mediated extraction, consolidating fact stores, and agentic control flows. Yet, their system-level behavior remains uncharacterized. We present the first systems characterization of agent memory. First, we introduce a system-oriented taxonomy classifying agent memory systems along four axes. Second, we build a phase-aware profiling harness attributing cost to construction, retrieval, and generation. Third, we characterize ten representative systems across two benchmark suites, uncovering how design choices shift cost across the write and read paths. Finally, we derive 10 system recommendations covering construction scheduling, capability floors, amortization via query volume, freshness-latency tradeoffs, and fleet-scale management.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a systems characterization of agent memory, introducing a taxonomy, profiling harness, and recommendations for optimizing agent memory systems.
AI.motivation: The increasing deployment of LLM agents on long-horizon tasks requires sustained reasoning over extended interaction histories, making persistent memory storage, retrieval, and updates crucial.
AI.method: The authors introduce a system-oriented taxonomy, a phase-aware profiling harness, and characterize ten representative agent memory systems across two benchmark suites.
AI.result: The study uncovers how design choices in agent memory systems shift cost across the write and read paths, and derives 10 system recommendations for optimization.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive characterization of agent memory systems, offering insights and recommendations for improving their design and efficiency.

title: PAR3D: A Unified 3D-MLLM with Part-Aware Representation for Scene Understanding
summary: Recent advances in 3D multimodal large language models (3D-MLLMs) have enabled unified solutions for 3D scene understanding tasks, including visual question answering, captioning, and referring segmentation. However, existing 3D-MLLMs remain largely object-centric, limiting their ability to model fine-grained part structures that are essential for embodied interaction with 3D environments. In this work, we present PAR3D, a unified part-aware 3D-MLLM framework that enables models to understand, reason about, and ground both objects and their parts in 3D scenes. To enable training and evaluation of part-aware 3D scene understanding, we introduce ScenePart, a synthetic 3D scene dataset with part-level annotations and language instructions. We further develop Part-Aware 3D Representation Learning to enrich 3D visual representations with fine-grained part-level semantics, and propose Hierarchical Segmentation Query Generation to ground part targets via hierarchical object-part queries. Extensive experiments show that our method substantially improves part-level question answering and referring segmentation, while also achieving strong performance across object-level vision-language tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PAR3D, a unified part-aware 3D multimodal large language model (3D-MLLM) framework that enables understanding, reasoning, and grounding of objects and their parts in 3D scenes.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D-MLLMs are largely object-centric, limiting their ability to model fine-grained part structures essential for embodied interaction with 3D environments.
AI.method: The authors propose Part-Aware 3D Representation Learning and Hierarchical Segmentation Query Generation to enrich 3D visual representations with part-level semantics and ground part targets.
AI.result: The method substantially improves part-level question answering and referring segmentation, while achieving strong performance across object-level vision-language tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PAR3D framework advances 3D scene understanding by incorporating part-aware capabilities, demonstrating improved performance in various tasks.

title: You Only Index Once: Cross-Layer Sparse Attention with Shared Routing
summary: Long-context inference in modern LLMs is increasingly constrained by decoding efficiency, especially in reasoning-heavy settings where models generate long intermediate chains of thought. Existing sparse attention methods often face a practical efficiency-quality trade-off. Structured block sparse methods typically provide stronger acceleration but incur noticeable quality loss, while token sparse methods are usually more accurate yet deliver limited end-to-end speedup because top-k routing over the full cache remains expensive. In this work, we propose cross-layer sparse attention (CLSA), which is built on top of KV-sharing architectures such as YOCO. The core idea is to share not only the KV cache across cross-decoder layers, but also the routing index. A single indexer computes token-level top-k selection once and reuses the resulting index across layers, thereby preserving the fine-grained selectivity of token sparse attention while amortizing the routing overhead. The resulting architecture improves all major inference bottlenecks jointly, including pre-filling, KV-cache storage, and long-context decoding. Experiments across short-context and long-context benchmarks show that CLSA is both accurate and efficient, achieving up to 7.6x decoding speedup and 17.1x overall throughput improvement at 128K context. These results suggest a more complete architectural solution for long-context LLMs that jointly advances model quality and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Cross-Layer Sparse Attention (CLSA) to improve the efficiency and accuracy of long-context inference in large language models (LLMs).
AI.motivation: Long-context inference in LLMs is constrained by decoding efficiency, particularly in reasoning-heavy settings. Existing sparse attention methods face a trade-off between efficiency and quality.
AI.method: The authors propose CLSA, which shares the KV cache and routing index across cross-decoder layers, preserving fine-grained selectivity while reducing routing overhead.
AI.result: CLSA achieves up to 7.6x decoding speedup and 17.1x overall throughput improvement at 128K context, with experiments showing both accuracy and efficiency improvements across short-context and long-context benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CLSA architecture provides a more complete solution for long-context LLMs, jointly advancing model quality and inference efficiency.

title: Vortex: Efficient and Programmable Sparse Attention Serving for AI Agents
summary: Sparse attention is becoming increasingly important for serving large language models (LLMs) as generation lengths continue to grow. However, deploying and evaluating new sparse attention algorithms at scale remains highly engineering-intensive, slowing both human researchers and AI agents in exploring the sparse attention design. To address this challenge, we present Vortex, a system that combines a Python-embedded frontend language atop a page-centric tensor abstraction for expressing a broad range of sparse attention algorithms, with an efficient backend tightly integrated into modern LLM serving stacks. Vortex enables rapid prototyping, deployment, and evaluation of sparse attention algorithms, effectively translating their theoretical efficiency gains into real-world throughput improvements. As a result, Vortex substantially accelerates the design and iteration of sparse attention algorithms. First, AI agents use Vortex to automatically generate and refine diverse algorithms, the best reaching up to $3.46\times$ higher throughput than full attention while preserving accuracy. Second, Vortex extends sparse attention to emerging architectures and very large models that are otherwise hard to experiment with, reaching up to $4.7\times$ higher throughput on the MLA-based GLM-4.7-Flash and $1.37\times$ on the 229B-parameter MiniMax-M2.7 on NVIDIA B200 GPUs.

AI.tldr: Vortex is a system for efficient design, deployment, and evaluation of sparse attention algorithms for large language models, achieving significant throughput improvements.
AI.motivation: The growing size of language models and generation lengths makes sparse attention increasingly important, but testing and evaluating new algorithms is engineering-intensive and time-consuming.
AI.method: Vortex combines a Python frontend with a page-centric tensor abstraction and an efficient backend integrated into modern LLM serving stacks.
AI.result: Vortex enables up to $3.46	imes$ higher throughput than full attention while preserving accuracy, and up to $4.7	imes$ and $1.37	imes$ higher throughput on specific large models.
AI.conclusion: Vortex substantially accelerates the design and iteration of sparse attention algorithms, facilitating their deployment in large language models.

title: Self-Augmenting Retrieval for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Discrete diffusion language models generate text by iteratively denoising an entire response in parallel. At each step, they predict tentative tokens for every masked position, committing the confident predictions to the output and discarding the unconfident ones. We show that the discarded tokens are in fact a useful lookahead signal for retrieval-augmented generation: even low-confidence tokens often surface salient entities early in the denoising trajectory, enabling retrieval of stronger evidence before the output is finalized. We exploit this through Self-Augmenting Retrieval for Diffusion Language Models (SARDI), a dynamic RAG framework that uses these lookahead tokens to guide retrieval during denoising. SARDI is training-free, retriever-agnostic, and applicable to any reasoning-capable discrete diffusion language model. Across five multi-hop QA benchmarks, SARDI outperforms current training-free diffusion and autoregressive retrieval baselines at up to $8\times$ higher throughput.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SARDI, a framework that enhances discrete diffusion language models by using low-confidence tokens to guide retrieval, improving performance in multi-hop QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The discarded low-confidence tokens in discrete diffusion language models contain useful information about salient entities, which can be leveraged to improve retrieval-augmented generation.
AI.method: SARDI, a dynamic retrieval-augmented generation framework that utilizes lookahead tokens from discrete diffusion language models to guide retrieval during denoising.
AI.result: SARDI outperforms current training-free diffusion and autoregressive retrieval baselines in five multi-hop QA benchmarks, achieving up to $8	imes$ higher throughput.
AI.conclusion: The proposed SARDI framework effectively leverages low-confidence tokens from discrete diffusion language models to improve retrieval-augmented generation, demonstrating superior performance and efficiency.

title: Benchmark Everything Everywhere All at Once
summary: Benchmarks are fundamental for evaluating and advancing LLMs and MLLMs by providing standardized and explicit measures of performance. However, their construction is labor-intensive and hard to reuse, raising concerns about sustainability and scalability. Moreover, existing benchmarks often quickly reach performance saturation after their release, resulting in insufficient discrimination among state-of-the-art models. To address these challenges, we introduce Benchmark Agent, a fully autonomous agentic system designed for benchmark building. Our framework orchestrates the complete benchmark construction pipeline, from user query analysis and subtask design to data annotation and quality control. To assess Benchmark Agent, we implement it to produce 15 representative benchmarks, spanning diverse evaluation scenarios, including text understanding, multimodal understanding, and domain-specific reasoning. Extensive experiments, including human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge assessment, and consistency checks, demonstrate Benchmark Agent can generate high-quality benchmark samples with minimal human involvement. More importantly, through continual evaluation, we observe several insightful findings, including that current models struggle with certain domain-specific reasoning tasks. We believe that rapidly evolving benchmarks can contribute significantly to the research community. The preview and code will be publicly available at the demo page and code repository.

AI.tldr: Introduces Benchmark Agent, an autonomous system for building benchmarks to evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), demonstrating its ability to generate high-quality benchmarks with minimal human involvement.
AI.motivation: The construction of benchmarks for LLMs and MLLMs is labor-intensive, hard to reuse, and often leads to performance saturation, making it difficult to discriminate among state-of-the-art models.
AI.method: Benchmark Agent is a fully autonomous agentic system that orchestrates the complete benchmark construction pipeline, including user query analysis, subtask design, data annotation, and quality control.
AI.result: Benchmark Agent generated 15 representative benchmarks spanning diverse evaluation scenarios, demonstrating its ability to produce high-quality benchmark samples with minimal human involvement, and revealing that current models struggle with certain domain-specific reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark Agent has the potential to contribute significantly to the research community by enabling the rapid evolution of benchmarks, which can help advance LLMs and MLLMs.

title: Operation-Guided Progressive Human-to-AI Text Transformation Benchmark for Multi-Granularity AI-Text Detection
comment: Our code and data are available at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/OpAI-Bench
summary: As AI writing assistants become increasingly integrated into real-world drafting and revision workflows, many documents are no longer purely human-written or AI-generated, but instead result from progressive human-AI co-editing. However, existing AI-text detection benchmarks largely focus on final outputs and provide limited understanding of how AI authorship signals emerge, accumulate, or disappear throughout the revision process. We introduce OpAI-Bench, an operation-guided benchmark for studying progressive human-to-AI text transformation across document, sentence, token, and span granularities. Starting from human-written documents, OpAI-Bench constructs nine sequentially revised versions for each sample under predefined AI coverage levels and five representative AI edit operations, covering four domains while preserving complete authorship provenance at multiple granularities. The benchmark supports comprehensive evaluation with 8 document-level detectors, 7 sentence-level detectors, and 2 fine-grained token/span-level detectors. Experiments reveal that AI-text detectability is governed not only by the proportion of AI-edited content, but also by edit operation, domain, and cumulative revision history. Interestingly, we notice that mixed-authorship intermediate versions are often harder to detect than both fully human and heavily AI-edited endpoints, exposing non-monotonic detection patterns missed by existing benchmarks. OpAI-Bench provides a controlled testbed for analyzing whether, when, and how AI-assisted writing becomes detectable under realistic progressive editing scenarios. Our code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/VILA-Lab/OpAI-Bench.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce OpAI-Bench, a benchmark for studying human-AI co-editing in text documents, and find that AI-text detectability depends on factors like AI-edited content proportion, edit operation, domain, and revision history.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-text detection benchmarks focus on final outputs, but not on the progressive human-AI co-editing process, which is increasingly common in real-world drafting and revision workflows.
AI.method: The authors construct OpAI-Bench, which includes human-written documents revised under predefined AI coverage levels and edit operations, and evaluate it with various detectors at different granularities.
AI.result: The experiments reveal that AI-text detectability is influenced by multiple factors, and mixed-authorship intermediate versions can be harder to detect than fully human or heavily AI-edited endpoints.
AI.conclusion: OpAI-Bench provides a controlled testbed for analyzing AI-assisted writing detectability under realistic progressive editing scenarios, and the authors make their code and benchmark available.

title: Goedel-Architect: Streamlining Formal Theorem Proving with Blueprint Generation and Refinement
summary: We introduce Goedel-Architect, an agentic framework for formal theorem proving in Lean 4 centered on blueprint generation and refinement. A blueprint is a dependency graph of definitions and lemmas that builds up to the main theorem. First, Goedel-Architect generates a blueprint of formally stated definitions and lemmas, along with declared dependencies. This blueprint is optionally guided by a natural language proof. Then, a tool-equipped Lean prover component closes each open lemma node in parallel using relevant dependencies. Failed lemmas in turn drive refinement of the global blueprint. This strategy contrasts with other mainstream approaches which use recursive lemma decomposition, and can inefficiently loop on dead-end strategies. Using the open-weight DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B-A13B) as the backbone, Goedel-Architect attains 99.2% pass@1 on MiniF2F-test and 75.6% pass@1 on PutnamBench. With an optional natural-language proof seeding the initial blueprint on the harder problems, we additionally close the remaining two MiniF2F-test problems (reaching 100%), lift PutnamBench to 88.8% (597/672), and solve 4/6 on IMO 2025, 11/12 on Putnam 2025, and 3/6 on USAMO 2026. This represents state-of-the-art performance for an open-source pipeline at a price point up to 500x less than comparable open-source pipelines.

AI.tldr: Goedel-Architect is an AI framework for formal theorem proving in Lean 4, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a novel blueprint generation and refinement approach.
AI.motivation: The motivation behind Goedel-Architect is to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of formal theorem proving, which is a crucial aspect of mathematics and computer science.
AI.method: Goedel-Architect uses a blueprint generation and refinement approach, where a dependency graph of definitions and lemmas is created and then refined through parallel lemma proving and optional natural language proof guidance.
AI.result: Goedel-Architect achieves 99.2% pass@1 on MiniF2F-test, 75.6% pass@1 on PutnamBench, and solves several problems on IMO 2025, Putnam 2025, and USAMO 2026, representing state-of-the-art performance for an open-source pipeline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework, Goedel-Architect, demonstrates a significant improvement in formal theorem proving capabilities, achieving state-of-the-art performance at a lower cost compared to other open-source pipelines.

title: MLEvolve: A Self-Evolving Framework for Automated Machine Learning Algorithm Discovery
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly applied to long-horizon tasks such as scientific discovery and machine learning engineering (MLE), where sustained self-evolution becomes a key capability. However, existing MLE agents suffer from inter-branch information isolation, memoryless search, and lack of hierarchical control, which together hinder long-horizon optimization. We present MLEvolve, an LLM-based self-evolving multi-agent framework for end-to-end machine learning algorithm discovery. By extending tree search to Progressive MCGS, MLEvolve enables cross-branch information flow through graph-based reference edges and gradually shifts the search from broad exploration to focused exploitation with an entropy-inspired progressive schedule. To allow the agent to evolve with accumulated experience, we introduce Retrospective Memory, which combines a cold-start domain knowledge base with a dynamic global memory for task-specific experience retrieval and reuse. For stable long-horizon iteration, we further decouple strategic planning from code generation with adaptive coding modes. Evaluation on MLE-Bench shows that MLEvolve achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple dimensions including average medal rate and valid submission rate under a 12-hour budget (half the standard runtime). Moreover, MLEvolve also outperforms specialized algorithm discovery methods including AlphaEvolve on mathematical algorithm optimization tasks, demonstrating strong cross-domain generalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/InternScience/MLEvolve.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MLEvolve, a framework for machine learning algorithm discovery using large language models, which improves upon existing methods by enabling cross-branch information flow, hierarchical control, and self-evolution.
AI.motivation: Existing machine learning engineering agents suffer from inter-branch information isolation, memoryless search, and lack of hierarchical control, hindering long-horizon optimization.
AI.method: The authors propose MLEvolve, an LLM-based self-evolving multi-agent framework that extends tree search to Progressive MCGS, introduces Retrospective Memory, and decouples strategic planning from code generation with adaptive coding modes.
AI.result: MLEvolve achieves state-of-the-art performance on MLE-Bench and outperforms specialized algorithm discovery methods, including AlphaEvolve, on mathematical algorithm optimization tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MLEvolve framework demonstrates strong cross-domain generalization and improves the efficiency of machine learning algorithm discovery.
